abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Drought is one of the most catastrophic abiotic stresses that affects global food production severely. The present work investigates the metabolic and physiological adaptation mechanisms in the xero‐halophyte <jats:italic>Haloxylon salicornicum</jats:italic> to counter the effects of drought. This xero‐halophyte can withstand a prolonged drought period of 14 days and recovered within 7 days of irrigation with minimal effects of drought on growth and physiological parameters. Photosynthetic parameters such as P<jats:sub>N</jats:sub>, g<jats:sub>s</jats:sub>, and E decreased significantly, whereas WUE increased under drought condition. Drought induces a significant decline in the Fv/Fm ratio. However, the value of Fv/Fm ratio successfully recovered within 7 days of the recovery period. Differential regulations of various antioxidative enzymes increase the drought tolerance potential of <jats:italic>H. salicornicum</jats:italic>. The metabolomic analysis of <jats:italic>H. salicornicum</jats:italic> shoot identified 63 metabolites: 43 significantly increased and 20 significantly decreased under drought conditions. These metabolites mainly include amino acids, organic acids, amines, sugar alcohols, sugars, fatty acids, alkaloids, and phytohormones. The metabolites that have a significant contribution towards drought tolerance include citric acid, malic acid, tartaric acid, <jats:sc>d</jats:sc>‐erythrose, glyceric acid, sucrose, pentanoic acid, <jats:sc>d</jats:sc>‐mannitol, ABA, and palmitic acid. KEGG pathway enrichment analysis showed that the vital drought‐responsive metabolic pathways mainly include galactose metabolism, aminoacyl‐tRNA biosynthesis, glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism, citrate cycle (TCA cycle), alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolism. This study offers comprehensive information on physiological, antioxidative and metabolic adaptations and overall drought tolerance mechanisms in <jats:italic>H. salicornicum</jats:italic>. abstract: <jats:title>SUMMARY</jats:title><jats:p>Attempts have been made to localize sodium and potassium with antimonate and cobaltinitrite reagents in <jats:italic>Suaeda</jats:italic> leaf segments by rapid aqueous and freeze‐substitution precipitation procedures and to localize chloride by freeze‐substitution precipitation with silver ions. Substantial sodium losses occurred from the tissue during both types of preparation although potassium and chloride losses were considerably reduced by the use of freeze‐substitution when compared with the rapid aqueous procedures. The losses during freeze‐substitution resulted from the required use of ethanol as substitution solvent (rather than acetone or diethyl ether, in which the reagents were much less soluble). Analytical electron microscopy showed that silver and cobaltinitrite specifically precipitated chloride and potassium respectively, but antimonate did not specifically precipitate sodium. The vacuoles were important sites of silver and antimonate deposits, although the chloroplasts were the major sites of cobaltinitrite localization. The value of these techniques in ion localization studies is discussed.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:sec>
                <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                <jats:p>Seed dimorphism has been thought to be a bet-hedging strategy that helps plants survive in the disturbed environment and has been widely studied for its ecological adaptation mechanism. Many studies showed that seed-associated microorganisms play an important role in enhancing plant fitness, but information regarding endophytic bacteria associated with dimorphic seeds is limited. This study explores the influence of seed coat structure and seed phytochemical properties on the community composition and diversity of endophytic bacteria of dimorphic seeds of <jats:italic>Suaeda glauca</jats:italic>. In this study, we used 16S rRNA high-throughput gene sequencing method to compare the community composition and bacterial diversity between brown and black seeds of <jats:italic>Suaeda glauca</jats:italic>.</jats:p>
              </jats:sec><jats:sec>
                <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                <jats:p>A significant difference was observed in seed coat structure and phytochemical properties between brown and black seeds of <jats:italic>S. glauca</jats:italic>. Total 9 phyla, 13 classes, 31 orders, 53 families, 102 genera were identified in the dimorphic seeds<jats:italic>.</jats:italic> The dominant phyla were <jats:italic>Proteobacteria</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>Firmicutes</jats:italic>, and <jats:italic>Actinobacteria.</jats:italic> The results showed that seed dimorphism had little impact on the diversity and richness of endophytic bacterial communities but significantly differs in the relative abundance of the bacterial community between brown and black seeds. At the phylum level, <jats:italic>Actinobacteria</jats:italic> tend to be enriched significantly in brown seeds. At the genus level, <jats:italic>Rhodococcus</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>Ralstonia</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>Pelomonas</jats:italic> and <jats:italic>Bradyrhizobium</jats:italic> tend to be enriched significantly in brown seeds, while <jats:italic>Marinilactibacillus</jats:italic> was mainly found in black seeds. Besides, brown seeds harbored a large number of bacteria with plant-growth-promoting traits, whereas black seeds presented bacteria with enzyme activities (i.e., pectinase, cellulolytic and xylanolytic activities).</jats:p>
              </jats:sec><jats:sec>
                <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                <jats:p>The endophytic bacterial community compositions were significantly different between dimorphic seeds of <jats:italic>Suaeda glauca</jats:italic>, and play an important role in the ecological adaptation of dimorphic seeds by performing different biological function roles. The endophytic bacterial communities of the dimorphic seeds may be influenced mainly by the seed coat structureand partly by the seed phytochemical characteristics. These findings provide valuable information for better understanding of the ecological adaptation strategy of dimorphic seeds in the disturbed environment.</jats:p>
              </jats:sec>
title: Insights into the endophytic bacterial community comparison and their potential role in the dimorphic seeds of halophyte Suaeda glauca
